messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was eight years old the night he watched his father’s fist meet his mother’s jaw. He had been hiding under the bed, fingers pressed over his mouth, listening to the thud of her body against the wall and the wet sound of her crying. He did not come out. He did not scream. He stayed there long after the front door slammed, and when he finally crawled into the light, his mother was on the kitchen floor, one eye already swelling shut. She told him not to tell anyone. He never did. For decades that silence sat inside him like a stone, but it was the guilt that grew into something alive—a voice that repeated, *You should have done something. You were a coward.* He forgave himself for nothing.

Now forty-five, Kwame works long days on a large vegetable farm in central California, driving a tractor through rows of tomatoes and bell peppers. He likes the noise of the engine because it drowns out his thoughts, but he cannot shake the feeling that something is watching him from the edge of the field, especially as the light fades. He has come to believe that he is no longer capable of happiness—that the boy who used to laugh with his cousins is gone, replaced by a man who measures every room for exits. The faith he once had in people, in any higher power that might have let that night happen, evaporated years ago. He is certain that if he lets his guard down for even a moment, harm will find him, and the reason he is certain is that he failed to protect the one person he loved most.

Because he cannot trust safety, even when his partner, Elena, tells him the front door is locked, Kwame remains hypervigilant. At night he finds it impossible to relax; he lies awake in the dark, listening to the creak of the house, the distant bark of a dog, his own pulse. He has learned that the only way to tolerate the watchfulness is to make sure he is never alone with another person. On the farm, that means he will not ride in the crew van if only one other worker is inside. He will wait until a third person arrives, or he will walk. When his supervisor asked him to help repair a broken irrigation line behind the tool shed—a task that would have put the two of them out of sight—Kwame made an excuse and left. He knows it looks strange, but the alternative feels impossible: to be alone with someone is to be vulnerable, and vulnerability invites disaster.

His mind, however, is rarely quiet. He spends hours replaying the scene from his childhood, but he does not stop at remembering—he imagines what he would do now to his father, if his father were still alive. The revenge fantasies give him a fleeting sense of control, yet they also keep his anger burning, and the anger feeds the guilt. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the images away during the day, but suppression only makes the memories sharper when they break through at night. The harder he works to block the past, the more his body stays on alert, scanning for threats that never quite arrive. And the constant scanning reinforces his belief that he is fundamentally broken, that happiness is something other people get to have.

The cycles have tightened over the past two years. Elena has begun to notice that Kwame no longer visits her family’s Sunday dinners, because the crowd forces him to stay near her the whole time, and being that close to so many people while feeling so exposed exhausts him. He has stopped going to the grocery store at night, even though it was his habit for years. At work, his colleagues have started to whisper that he is antisocial or strange. He knows he is losing ground. What finally brought him to the clinic was not the isolation itself but a moment two weeks ago when he was driving the tractor after dusk and saw a figure at the edge of the field—just a farmhand checking a fence—and he slammed the brakes so hard the engine stalled. He sat in the cab with his hands shaking, convinced for ten full seconds that it was his father. He could not sleep for three nights afterward. When Elena found him staring at the bedroom door at 3 AM, she asked him to get help. He agreed, not because he thinks talking could change anything, but because he is afraid of what he might do if the revenge fantasies ever feel like the only way out.
